1.stem: [Academic Talk — Marine Biology] What does the professor imply about how next year's survey will be run?

options.A: Divers will take over from the towed cameras across the roughest stretches of seabed
options.B: It will work from a chartered trawler rather than the institute's own research vessel
options.C: It will be run jointly with the neighboring country's fisheries institute for the first time
options.D: It will cover the abandoned bank one final time before dropping it from the rotation

2.stem: [Academic Talk — Musicology] Why does the professor bring up the court at Casperi?

options.A: Its payment records show the suites were played there within a few seasons of their composition
options.B: The printed dedication names its duke rather than Welden's, a puzzle the professor returns to
options.C: A letter sent from there gives the one contemporary description of Fantin directing a performance
options.D: Its far larger string band makes a contrast with the modest forces the suites require

3.stem: [Academic Talk — Urban History] What does the professor say the rent series shows happened in the old center once the ring opened?

options.A: Rents fell across the center as wealthy households moved out toward the new edge
options.B: Rents held level, with no break in the series that the demolition could account for
options.C: Rents climbed once the carting traffic shifted away from the center's narrow streets
options.D: Rents split, climbing along the street fronts while sinking in the courts behind them

4.stem: [Academic Talk — Urban History] Why does the professor quote from the visiting engineer's report of 1831?

options.A: It preserves the last full survey of the fortifications before demolition began
options.B: Its author later laid out the ring promenade, and in it his own ideas can be seen taking shape
options.C: Its sketches show how the wrecking crews actually went about bringing the towers down
options.D: Its flattering dedication shows how such reports doubled as bids for a city's patronage

5.stem: [Academic Talk — Glaciology] What is the professor's central claim about why the glacier's front has been advancing?

options.A: Snowy winters two decades back are arriving at the terminus now as a slow-moving bulge
options.B: A change at the bed is letting the ice slide forward faster, without any overall gain in mass
options.C: A tributary arm that had stagnated has reconnected and is feeding the trunk again
options.D: A bank of sediment building up in the water ahead is letting the ice push outward

6.stem: [Academic Talk — Musicology] What does the professor suggest the editors will do about the missing second-violin book?

options.A: Reconstruct its lines from what survives and mark the reconstruction as editorial
options.B: Acquire an amateur copy reported in a private collection, for which talks are underway
options.C: Hold the suites it touches back for a final volume, once the rest are out
options.D: Print the affected suites as they stand, with that line simply left out

7.stem: [Academic Talk — Marine Biology] Why does the professor mention the jars of preserved samples in the institute's basement?

options.A: They show the fish were already spawning there seventy years before monitoring began
options.B: They nearly went out in a renovation, the professor's case for why collections need keepers
options.C: They hold enough material to check whether the fish themselves have changed over the decades
options.D: They turned out to be mislabeled in a way that sent two earlier studies astray

8.stem: [Academic Talk — Astronomy] What is the professor's central claim about what is producing the gap?

options.A: The grains there have grown too large to show up, so the zone is dark without being empty
options.B: It lies where one of the abundant ices condenses onto the grains, changing how they clump and drift
options.C: A warp closer in throws a shadow outward, so the zone is poorly lit rather than cleared
options.D: A companion embedded in the disk is sweeping that zone clear as it goes around the star

9.stem: [Academic Talk — Paleontology] How does the professor respond to the isotope study's conclusion that the animals had traveled from far away?

options.A: He backs it, and wants the same measurements run on the other species in the quarry
options.B: He doubts the method itself for material this old, since burial slowly rewrites the signal
options.C: He trusts the chemistry but reads the signal as a change in local water, not as travel
options.D: He sets it aside because its reference values come from a basin with a different geology

10.stem: [Academic Talk — Anthropology] What did the team's fieldwork indicate about how a band's worth is judged?

options.A: Chiefly by age: darkened older pieces count above anything freshly made
options.B: Chiefly by handle: elders roll the cloth between their fingers and grade the tightness
options.C: Chiefly by design: certain named motifs outrank the rest, whatever the weaving's quality
options.D: Chiefly by biography: who wove it and through which households it has already passed

11.stem: [Academic Talk — Astronomy] What does the professor suggest the team intends to do next?

options.A: Hold off on further observing until an upgrade to the receivers sharpens the array
options.B: Point the identical setup at a set of comparable young stars to learn how common this is
options.C: Put the data out ahead of their own paper so that rival groups can work on it too
options.D: Approach the array's time committee about mapping the disk's faint outer reaches

12.stem: [Academic Talk — Paleontology] What did the bone-by-bone mapping of the main layer reveal?

options.A: Complete individuals lie at the middle of the bed, with scattered bone toward its edges
options.B: The animals lie in tight clusters of three or four, with clear ground between the groups
options.C: The small elements are gone throughout, right down to the bones of the feet
options.D: The skeletons share one orientation, lined up nose to tail along a single bearing

13.stem: [Academic Talk — Marine Biology] What did the professor say the tag returns showed about where the fish went after the move?

options.A: The oldest fish kept turning up at the old site for years after the rest had gone
options.B: The tagged fish scattered across half a dozen lesser grounds without settling anywhere
options.C: The returns split by age, the older fish at one site and the younger at the other
options.D: Fish tagged at the old site were being caught over the new one within a single season

14.stem: [Academic Talk — Paleontology] What does the professor indicate the project will do next?

options.A: Cover the exposure back over and hold it in reserve until techniques improve
options.B: Put up a permanent shelter so that excavation can continue through the year
options.C: Pump out the flooded section and open it for the first time in a century
options.D: Shift the search to the surrounding plain, prospecting for other beds of the same age

15.stem: [Academic Talk — Urban History] How does the professor characterize the city council's handling of the demolition?

options.A: As directionless, reversing itself so often that no plan can be credited with the outcome
options.B: As more far-sighted than critics allowed, spacing the work over decades so the city carried no debt from it
options.C: As largely reactive, ratifying openings that townspeople had already forced in the walls
options.D: As self-serving, steering the contracts to its own members' firms at three times the first estimate

16.stem: [Academic Talk — Economic History] How does the professor treat the long-standing explanation that a ring of merchants caused the spike by holding grain back?

options.A: He credits it, and believes the ring's own papers sit unrecognized in a notary's files
options.B: He dismisses it, reckoning the quantities a ring could control were too small to matter for long
options.C: He dismisses it on the storage registers, which show the suspected houses selling steadily throughout
options.D: He inverts it: merchants did withhold, but as a reaction to the spike rather than its cause

17.stem: [Academic Talk — Glaciology] Why does the professor talk about the Ravnas farm?

options.A: Its account books fix the season when the ice first became visible from the valley floor
options.B: A grazing dispute fought from the farm left sworn statements of where the ice margin stood
options.C: A sketch made from its yard is the earliest surviving picture of the glacier
options.D: Its family cut and sold ice to towns downriver, a trade the professor lingers over

18.stem: [Academic Talk — Musicology] What is the professor's position on the claim that the suites were composed for actual dancing?

options.A: He accepts it, but on the strength of fee entries in the court ledger rather than anything in the scores
options.B: He accepts it, mainly because the repeat schemes line up with the figures of period choreographies
options.C: He rejects it, arguing that the tempo markings would leave the steps impossible to execute
options.D: He divides the repertory: the opening movements were for the ballroom, the closing ones for listening at table

19.stem: [Academic Talk — Anthropology] What does the professor imply about the weaving of the bands today?

options.A: It has moved to market towns downriver, whose products are traded back into the valley
options.B: It continues, but the bands now pass as festival gifts rather than in marriage payments
options.C: It carries on for everyday cloth, while the marriage designs themselves have been retired
options.D: It ended within living memory, and the bands that survive circulate as heirlooms

20.stem: [Academic Talk — Astronomy] Why does the professor bring up the Kestler program's observations of the star?

options.A: The new measurements had to be tied to its calibration stars before anyone would trust them
options.B: It found the disk in the first place, as a by-product of a search for something unrelated
options.C: Its images, blurry as they are, show the feature was already present twenty years ago
options.D: It reported the disk as featureless, a miss the professor uses to mark how far instruments have come

21.stem: [Academic Talk — Urban History] According to the tax rolls, who moved onto the cleared ground along the ring first?

options.A: Innkeepers, catching travelers who once had to lodge outside the old gates
options.B: Market gardeners, who held their plots cheaply for a generation before builders arrived
options.C: The hospital and two church schools, which took the largest parcels between them
options.D: Weaving shops that wanted the drying yards they could not fit inside the town

22.stem: [Academic Talk — Economic History] What did the price series drawn from the ledgers show about how the spike spread?

options.A: It jumped from town to town in no geographic order anyone has been able to find
options.B: It struck the ports first and barely took hold in the upland districts
options.C: It appeared across the whole region within days, with no lag worth the name
options.D: It began in the inland market towns and reached the coast weeks later

23.stem: [Academic Talk — Glaciology] What does the professor imply the team plans to do next field season?

options.A: Mount an automatic camera on the spur facing the front to record it day by day
options.B: Carry the line of survey stakes higher up the glacier than it has ever gone
options.C: Keep the field station manned year-round for the first time
options.D: Re-photograph the front from the ridge points the 1938 photographers used

24.stem: [Academic Talk — Economic History] According to the letters, what did the partners do while prices were at their height?

options.A: They stepped out of grain for the season and moved their capital into timber
options.B: They sold the firm's stocks early and watched most of the rise from the sidelines
options.C: They took a commission to buy on the city's account instead of trading for themselves
options.D: They kept the ships working as carriers, hauling other houses' cargoes for a fee

25.stem: [Academic Talk — Paleontology] Why does the professor tell the story of the quarry's discovery by railway workers?

options.A: The railway cut sliced the deposit from top to bottom, a view no planned dig could have afforded
options.B: Crates of specimens went to buyers abroad, and tracing them has become a project in itself
options.C: Letters the workers wrote settle exactly which layer the first specimens came out of
options.D: The first collectors kept no notes, which is why the bed's upper part cannot now be placed

26.stem: [Academic Talk — Anthropology] Why does the professor spend time on the district officer's inventory of 1902?

options.A: It sets down exchange rates against livestock, the earliest written valuations there are
options.B: It shows examples had already traveled well beyond the valley by the time it was compiled
options.C: It preserves names of pattern types that can no longer be matched to any surviving band
options.D: It was drawn up for tax purposes, a reason to be wary of taking its figures at face value

27.stem: [Academic Talk — Anthropology] What is the professor's judgment of Marovic's account of the exchange system?

options.A: Systematically misled: his informants gave him the version reserved for outsiders
options.B: Split down the middle: exact on the weaving, unreliable on everything to do with exchange
options.C: Sound in the main: it matches what the team recorded once his invented vocabulary is set aside
options.D: Out of time: he took the fashion of his own decade for the valley's ancient practice

28.stem: [Academic Talk — Astronomy] What did the new Aldan Array observations show about the gap in the disk?

options.A: It is nearly twice as wide as the models had it, a belt rather than a groove
options.B: It lies a good deal farther out from the star than the models had put it
options.C: What looked like one opening is actually two narrow ones, separated by a bright strand
options.D: Its inner boundary is sharply cut while the outer one fades away by degrees

29.stem: [Academic Talk — Glaciology] According to the professor, what did the lake cores show about how long the 1870s advance lasted?

options.A: It came as two pushes, separated by a lull long enough for soil to begin forming
options.B: It went on for roughly thirty years, holding the lower valley for a full generation
options.C: It lasted the better part of a half century, much as the oldest maps imply
options.D: It ran its course in under a decade, far more briefly than had been assumed

30.stem: [Academic Talk — Economic History] Why does the professor work through a single page of the Ostrand ledgers in class?

options.A: To show the notation that has to be decoded before any of the totals can be used
options.B: To show how one entry can be followed out into the firm's correspondence
options.C: To show the change of hand that marks where the founder's son took over the books
options.D: To show that barter deals were entered right alongside the cash sales

31.stem: [Academic Talk — Marine Biology] What is the professor's main point about why the spawning grounds moved?

options.A: The bloom the larvae feed on comes earlier now, and the new place matches its timing
options.B: A warm current now crosses the old ground during the spawning season
options.C: Gravel on the old ground has been silting over, and the eggs need clean stone
options.D: A seal colony established itself on the skerries nearby and hunts the gathering shoals

32.stem: [Academic Talk — Musicology] What did the professor say the wear on the manuscript parts suggested about how they were used?

options.A: The set seems to have been in steady use across its whole span, over a period of years
options.B: There is little sign of use, and the parts may have served as a presentation set rather than working copies
options.C: Most of the marking appears to come from later library handling rather than from performers
options.D: The earlier suites saw heavy use, while the later ones look barely to have been opened
